explanation: `instance` is not declared `volatile`. Under the Java Memory Model, `instance = new Singleton()` can be split into (1) allocate memory, (2) assign the reference, (3) run the constructor — and without a `volatile` field or other memory barrier, steps 2 and 3 can be reordered from another thread's point of view. A second thread executing the outer `if (instance == null)` check outside the lock can see a non-null reference whose constructor hasn't finished running yet, and start using a partially-initialized object. Adding `volatile` (or using a holder class / atomic reference) prevents that reordering.
prompt: This double-checked-locking singleton has a subtle threading bug. What is it?
choices: The `instance` field isn't declared `volatile`, so under the Java Memory Model a thread can observe a non-null but only partially-constructed `Singleton` due to instruction reordering during construction
The outer `if (instance == null)` check outside the synchronized block is redundant and should be removed since the inner check already guards against races
The synchronized block should wrap the entire `getInstance` method rather than just the initialization check
The inner null check inside the synchronized block will always be true, since two threads can never enter the block at the same time
